title: Tree Hidden Inside a Tree
statement:
You get the roots of two non-empty binary trees, root and sub. Return true if some node of root is the top of a copy of sub: that node together with all of its descendants has exactly the same shape and values as sub.

Matching the top part is not enough; the copy has to end where sub ends. root itself counts as one of its own nodes.

Trees are written in level order with null for a missing child.

examples.why: The first 3 has children 1 and 2, so it does not match. The second 3 has children 1 and 4, an exact copy. Do not stop at the first node whose value fits.

examples.in: root = [8, 6, 9, 2, 7, null, null, null, null, null, 1], sub = [6, 2, 7]
examples.why: Node 6 starts out right (children 2 and 7), but 7 has an extra child 1 in root. A match must include everything below the node.
The root 4 also has a right child, so it fails. The lower 4, with only a left child 9, is the copy.

constraints: Each tree is at most 500 levels deep
hints: You already know how to tell whether two trees are identical. Where in root could a copy of sub start?
Try every node of root as a starting point and run the identical-tree check from there. Remember that the check must compare null children too.

For a faster version, write both trees as strings in pre-order with a marker for every null child and a separator before every value. Then sub is inside root exactly when its string is a substring of root's string.

explain.intuition:
A copy of sub has to start somewhere, at some node of root. So try them all: walk through root, and at each node ask "is the tree starting here identical to sub?" The identical check is the lockstep walk from comparing two trees, and it is what enforces the "everything below must match" rule: an extra child in root meets a null in sub and fails. That costs O(n · m) in the worst case, which is fine at these sizes, and most starting points fail after one or two steps.

There is also a string trick. Write a tree in pre-order and record every missing child as #: that string pins down the shape exactly, and the subtree under any node is one contiguous slice of it. So sub occurs in root exactly when its string occurs in root's string. Put a separator before every token, or the value 2 will be found inside the value 12. With a linear-time substring search (KMP), this runs in O(n + m).
steps: Write same(x, y): both null → true; one null → false; values differ → false; else both child pairs must be the same.
Visit every node of root (recursion or a stack).
At each node, if same(node, sub), return true.
If no node matches, return false.
String version: serialize both trees as ,val tokens in pre-order with ,# for null, then test whether the sub string is a substring of the root string.
pitfalls: Stopping at the first node whose value equals sub's root. Duplicate values are allowed, like in the first example.
Checking only that sub's nodes appear in root, ignoring the nulls. Then an extra child in root, as in the second example, is missed.
Serializing without null markers or without a separator before each value. Without markers different shapes collide; without the leading separator [12] seems to contain [2].

complexity.time: O(n · m) for the direct check, O(n + m) with serialization and a linear substring search

solutions.title: Check every node as a starting point
solutions.idea: Walk root; at each node run the identical-tree check against sub.

solutions.title: Serialize both, then search for a substring
solutions.idea: Pre-order with ',#' for every null and ',' before every value. A subtree is a contiguous slice of that string, so the question becomes a substring search.
solutions.time: O(n + m) with a linear search

followups: Instead of strings, give every subtree a hash computed from its value and its children's hashes. What goes wrong with collisions, and how do you guard against them?
Count how many nodes of root are the top of a copy of sub.
